questions.stem: An 81 year old woman taking apixaban for atrial fibrillation has had three falls in the last month. Over 2 weeks she has become increasingly muddled, with a headache. Her daughter says some hours she is drowsy and others she is almost normal. She has mild weakness of her left arm. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and irregular, BP 154/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Delirium secondary to urinary tract infection
questions.e: Repeated falls on an anticoagulant followed by progressive confusion, headache, fluctuating consciousness and focal weakness is a chronic subdural haemorrhage.

clues: some hours she is drowsy and others she is almost normal
mild weakness of her left arm
steps.x: Elderly, anticoagulated, falls, fluctuating confusion, focal sign.

elim: Gradual memory decline over years, without fluctuating consciousness or focal weakness.
She is afebrile, and delirium does not explain the headache and focal weakness after falls.
Fluctuates, but over months to years with hallucinations and parkinsonism, and no headache or focal weakness.
Sudden onset, not progressive confusion over 2 weeks.

steps.x: B: Chronic subdural haemorrhage. Falls + anticoagulation + fluctuating GCS = chronic subdural.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man has a crescent-shaped collection over the right cerebral convexity on CT head 2 weeks after a fall. The radiologist reports an extra-axial collection that crosses the coronal suture. A student asks exactly where the blood lies. His GCS is 14 and BP 150/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Between which layers is the blood most likely to be?
o: Inner table of the skull and dura mater
Subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia
questions.e: A subdural haemorrhage is a collection of blood between the dura and the arachnoid mater; it crosses suture lines.

steps.x: Crescentic extra-axial collection crossing sutures.

elim: The extradural space, limited by sutures.
Not a real space; blood here would be intracerebral.
A subgaleal haematoma outside the skull.
Where berry aneurysms bleed; blood fills sulci and cisterns.

steps.x: A: Dura mater and arachnoid mater. Subdural = between dura and arachnoid.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man with known cerebral atrophy falls and bumps his head. Ten days later he is drowsy and confused. CT head shows a crescentic collection over the left hemisphere crossing the suture lines. He is not anticoagulated. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 146/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely source of the bleeding?
questions.e: Subdural haemorrhage is most commonly caused by tearing of the bridging veins that run from the cerebral cortex across the subdural space to the venous sinuses.

steps.x: Crescentic collection after minor trauma in an atrophic brain.

elim: Cause deep intracerebral haemorrhage in hypertension.
The source of extradural haemorrhage, which does not cross sutures.
Bleeds into the subarachnoid space.
Sinus injury is rare; the cortical veins draining into it are the usual source.

steps.x: A: Bridging veins. Subdural bleeding = torn bridging veins.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man falls down a flight of stairs and hits his head. Three hours later he is drowsy with a GCS of 12. He takes warfarin. His pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 172/90 mmHg. An urgent non-contrast CT head is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the CT head?
o: Hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns
Hyperdense crescent-shaped collection crossing suture lines with sulcal effacement
Hyperdense lens-shaped collection limited by suture lines
Hypodense crescent-shaped collection crossing suture lines
Isodense crescent-shaped collection crossing suture lines
questions.e: An acute subdural is a hyperdense crescent-shaped extra-axial collection that crosses suture lines, often with sulcal effacement; density falls with time.

steps.x: Hours after trauma on warfarin: an acute subdural.

elim: Subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Extradural haemorrhage.
A chronic subdural, typically over 2 to 3 weeks old.
A subacute subdural, days to weeks old.

steps.x: B: Hyperdense crescent-shaped collection crossing suture lines with sulcal effacement. Acute subdural = hyperdense crescent; subacute isodense; chronic hypodense.

questions.stem: An 84 year old woman fell 10 days ago. She now has a headache and is slower than usual. Her GCS is 14. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 148/84 mmHg. The CT head is initially reported as 'no obvious haemorrhage' but a senior radiologist notes effaced sulci and a subtle shift of the midline on one side.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the initial report?
questions.e: Subdural density changes with time: hyperdense when acute, isodense when subacute (similar to brain, easily missed), hypodense when chronic.

steps.x: Days to weeks old, almost invisible except for mass effect.

elim: Would be bright and obvious.
Would be darker than brain and usually seen; she is only 10 days out.
Sulcal effacement and midline shift are abnormal.
Causes enlarged ventricles, not unilateral sulcal effacement and shift.

steps.x: D: An isodense subacute subdural haemorrhage. Subacute subdural is isodense and easily missed.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man is hit on the head with a bottle. CT head shows an extra-axial collection over the right frontoparietal region. The consultant asks the registrar which feature on the scan best confirms that this is a subdural rather than an extradural haemorrhage. His GCS is 14.
questions.q: Which CT feature best distinguishes a subdural haemorrhage?
o: Biconvex collection limited by suture lines
questions.e: A subdural is crescent-shaped and crosses suture lines; an extradural is lens-shaped and limited by them because the dura is attached at sutures.

steps.x: Separate two extra-axial collections.

elim: More typical of extradural haemorrhage.
Extradural haemorrhage.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Both acute subdural and extradural blood are hyperdense.

steps.x: D: Crescent-shaped collection crossing suture lines. Subdural crosses sutures (crescent); extradural does not (lens).

questions.stem: A 77 year old man with a known acute subdural haemorrhage over the left hemisphere is being observed on the ward. Over 2 hours he becomes increasingly drowsy and his GCS falls from 14 to 9. His pulse rate is 52 bpm, BP 188/96 mmHg and respiratory rate 10 breaths per minute.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Dilated left pupil with right-sided weakness
Dilated right pupil with right-sided weakness
questions.e: As the haematoma expands it causes unequal pupils (ipsilateral third nerve compression) and contralateral hemiparesis, late signs with a Cushing's response.

clues: pulse rate is 52 bpm, BP 188/96 mmHg
steps.x: Expanding left subdural with falling GCS and Cushing's response.

elim: Pontine haemorrhage or opioids.
The pupil dilates on the side of the haematoma, which is the left.
Suggests lateral medullary or carotid pathology.
Indicates functional weakness.

steps.x: B: Dilated left pupil with right-sided weakness. Late subdural signs: ipsilateral dilated pupil, contralateral weakness.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man is admitted with a subdural haemorrhage after a minor fall. He drinks 60 units of alcohol a week. He has gout, a previous appendicectomy, well-controlled asthma and hypothyroidism. He takes no anticoagulants. His BP is 146/84 mmHg. CT also shows generalised cerebral atrophy.
questions.q: Which feature of his history most increased his risk of subdural haemorrhage?
questions.e: Chronic alcohol excess causes brain atrophy and falls, and impairs clotting; atrophy stretches bridging veins, making them vulnerable to shearing.

steps.x: Heavy alcohol use with atrophy.

elim: Not a risk factor.
Not a risk factor.
Not a risk factor.
Not a risk factor.

steps.x: A: Chronic alcohol use. Risk factors: age over 65, trauma, anticoagulants, coagulopathy, alcohol, atrophy.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman bumped her head on a kitchen cupboard 6 weeks ago and thought nothing of it. Over the last 2 weeks she has had a worsening headache, has vomited twice and her husband says her speech is mildly slurred. She is drowsy. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 150/86 mmHg. She takes aspirin.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A chronic subdural can present several weeks after a minor head injury, with gradual headache, vomiting, slurred speech and drowsiness, because venous blood accumulates slowly.

steps.x: Minor injury weeks ago, then slowly progressive symptoms.

elim: Presents within hours, often after a lucid interval, with a skull fracture.
Sudden onset, not progressive over 2 weeks.
Gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and dementia, without headache and vomiting after an injury.
Presents with a sudden thunderclap headache.

steps.x: A: Chronic subdural haemorrhage. Chronic subdural can present weeks after a trivial bump.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man was diagnosed with a stroke by his GP 10 days ago after developing weakness of his right leg. Since then the weakness has slowly worsened and spread to his right arm, and he has a constant headache and is sleeping more. He fell from a ladder 4 weeks ago. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 142/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A progressive hemiparesis with headache and drowsiness weeks after a fall is a subdural haemorrhage, a classic stroke mimic.

clues: fell from a ladder 4 weeks ago
steps.x: Progressive focal weakness, headache, drowsiness, earlier fall.

elim: Sudden onset with a maximal deficit, not progressive over 10 days.
Progresses over months without headache or drowsiness.
Resolves within 24 hours.
Stepwise cognitive decline, not progressive hemiparesis with headache and drowsiness.

steps.x: C: Subdural haemorrhage. A 'stroke' that keeps worsening after a fall: think subdural.

questions.stem: An 87 year old man has a chronic subdural haemorrhage that has been managed conservatively for 4 weeks. Yesterday he suddenly became more drowsy, with new weakness of his left arm. He has not fallen again. His pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 168/90 mmHg. A repeat non-contrast CT head is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the CT head?
o: Crescentic collection of mixed density with scattered hypodense and hyperdense areas
Hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns
Lens-shaped hyperdense collection limited by sutures
Uniformly hypodense crescentic collection unchanged from before
Wedge-shaped hypodensity in the right MCA territory
questions.e: A chronic subdural can rebleed and enlarge; acute-on-chronic subdural shows mixed density, with fresh hyperdense blood among scattered hypodense areas.

steps.x: Sudden worsening of a known chronic subdural.

elim: Subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Extradural haemorrhage.
Would not explain his sudden deterioration.
An ischaemic infarct, not a change in a known subdural.

steps.x: A: Crescentic collection of mixed density with scattered hypodense and hyperdense areas. Acute-on-chronic subdural = mixed density.

questions.stem: A 90 year old woman in a care home taking rivaroxaban has been sleepier and more confused for 5 days. Staff found her on the floor a week ago. She has a bruise on her forehead. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 152/88 mmHg. Urine dipstick is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: An urgent non-contrast CT head is the gold standard for subdural haemorrhage, showing a crescent-shaped collection crossing suture lines.

steps.x: Anticoagulated, fall, fluctuating drowsiness and confusion.

elim: Contrast is not needed to see blood and may hide it.
Dangerous with a possible mass lesion.
Too slow; this needs urgent imaging.
Shows fractures, not intracranial blood.

steps.x: E: Urgent non-contrast CT head. Suspected subdural: urgent non-contrast CT head.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man has an acute subdural haemorrhage after falling off a bicycle. He has a headache and his GCS is 14. He is not anticoagulated. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 148/84 mmHg. The neurosurgical registrar reviews the non-contrast CT head to decide whether he needs an operation.
questions.q: Which CT finding most strongly indicates the need for surgery?
o: Midline shift of more than 5 mm
questions.e: Acute subdural surgery is indicated for raised ICP, midline shift of more than 5 mm on CT, or deteriorating focal neurology.

clues: decide whether he needs an operation
steps.x: Which feature makes it surgical?

elim: Not an indication for surgery.
Present in all subdurals.
Typical of all subdurals.
Simply means the blood is acute.

steps.x: E: Midline shift of more than 5 mm. Acute subdural surgery: raised ICP, midline shift over 5 mm, worsening neurology.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has a 4 mm acute subdural haemorrhage after a fall. She is not anticoagulated, her GCS is 15 and neurological examination is normal. There is no midline shift. The neurosurgeons recommend conservative management with regular neurological observations.
questions.q: Which investigation is most appropriate for ongoing monitoring?
questions.e: Small asymptomatic acute subdurals are managed with close observation, regular examination and serial CT scanning.

steps.x: Small, asymptomatic, observed.

elim: Dangerous and does not assess the collection.
For seizures.
Shows fractures, not the haematoma.
Looks for vascular lesions, not haematoma size.

steps.x: E: Serial non-contrast CT head. Small asymptomatic subdural: observe with serial CT.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation has a symptomatic acute subdural haemorrhage on CT after a fall. His GCS is 13. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and irregular, BP 156/88 mmHg. The neurosurgical team asks for a blood test before deciding on reversal and surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most important blood test?
questions.e: On warfarin, the INR shows the degree of anticoagulation; ongoing anticoagulant effect increases haematoma expansion, so it is reversed before referral and surgery.

steps.x: Warfarin and a bleed: measure the anticoagulant effect.

elim: No sign of infection.
Does not change management.
Looks for rhabdomyolysis after a long lie, not bleeding risk.
Not useful in a confirmed bleed.

steps.x: E: International normalised ratio. Warfarin + subdural: check INR and reverse.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with alcohol dependence is brought in by police after being found wandering. He smells of alcohol. Over 12 hours on the ward his GCS fluctuates between 11 and 15 and he has a bruise behind his right ear. His capillary glucose is 5.6 mmol/L. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 142/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Fluctuating consciousness after possible head trauma in an alcohol-dependent patient needs an urgent non-contrast CT head to look for a subdural.

steps.x: Alcohol, head injury, fluctuating GCS.

elim: Fluctuating GCS must not be blamed on alcohol until a bleed is excluded.
For seizures; this is not first.
Dangerous before imaging with a fluctuating GCS.
Slower and less available; CT is the gold standard for acute blood.

steps.x: E: Non-contrast CT head. Never blame fluctuating GCS on alcohol: CT head.

questions.stem: An 82 year old woman taking warfarin has a symptomatic subdural haemorrhage on CT with headache and confusion. Her GCS is 14 and she has mild right arm weakness. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 150/86 mmHg. She is in a district general hospital.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Continue warfarin and repeat CT in 1 week
Reverse anticoagulation and refer to neurosurgery
Stop warfarin and discharge with GP follow-up
Switch warfarin to low molecular weight heparin
questions.e: A symptomatic subdural needs anticoagulation reversal and referral to neurosurgery.

steps.x: Symptomatic bleed on an anticoagulant.

elim: An active bleed on warfarin needs reversal.
Antiplatelets worsen bleeding.
She is symptomatic and needs specialist care.
Still anticoagulated.

steps.x: B: Reverse anticoagulation and refer to neurosurgery. Symptomatic subdural: reverse anticoagulation and refer to neurosurgery.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man falls from a ladder. On arrival his GCS is 9 and his left pupil is larger than the right. His pulse rate is 58 bpm, BP 176/94 mmHg and respiratory rate 12 breaths per minute. His airway has been secured. CT head shows a 14 mm hyperdense crescentic collection over the left hemisphere with 9 mm midline shift.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: An acute subdural with midline shift over 5 mm and deteriorating neurology needs craniotomy with clot evacuation and coagulation of bleeding vessels.

steps.x: Acute, large, shift and a falling GCS.

elim: The first-line operation for chronic, liquefied subdurals, not acute clotted blood.
For small asymptomatic subdurals only.
A temporising measure, not definitive.
Dangerous with midline shift.

steps.x: C: Craniotomy with clot evacuation. Acute surgical subdural = craniotomy; chronic = burr hole.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man has a large acute subdural haemorrhage after a road traffic collision. During craniotomy and clot evacuation, the surgeons find the underlying brain is very swollen and bulging out of the wound, so the bone flap cannot be replaced. His intracranial pressure remains high.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate procedure?
questions.e: Large acute subdurals with severe brain swelling may need decompressive craniectomy, leaving the bone flap out to allow the brain to swell.

steps.x: Brain swelling after evacuation of an acute subdural.

elim: For chronic subdurals.
Secures intracranial aneurysms.
Dangerous with raised ICP.
Treats hydrocephalus.

steps.x: B: Decompressive craniectomy. Large acute subdural with swelling: decompressive craniectomy.

questions.stem: An 83 year old man taking warfarin has a 3 week history of worsening headache and confusion after a fall. His GCS has dropped from 15 to 13 over 2 days. His pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 160/88 mmHg. CT head shows a 20 mm hypodense crescentic collection over the right hemisphere with 7 mm midline shift.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Reverse anticoagulation and perform burr hole craniostomy
questions.e: A symptomatic chronic subdural with deterioration and mass effect needs burr hole craniostomy plus anticoagulation reversal.

steps.x: Chronic, deteriorating, mass effect, on warfarin.

elim: He is deteriorating with mass effect and is anticoagulated.
Craniotomy is for acute subdurals, and reversal must come first.
For large acute subdurals with brain swelling.
Does not drain the collection.

steps.x: E: Reverse anticoagulation and perform burr hole craniostomy. Chronic subdural surgery = burr hole + reversal.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has an acute subdural haemorrhage with signs of raised ICP after a fall. His GCS is 7 and he has been intubated. His pulse rate is 54 bpm and BP 190/100 mmHg. The nearest neurosurgical theatre is unavailable for the next hour while transfer is arranged. The ICU team considers a temporary measure.
questions.q: Which statement about hyperventilation is most accurate?
o: It is contraindicated in raised ICP
It is the definitive treatment when surgery is unavailable
It lowers ICP by causing hypercapnia
It lowers ICP for a short time only by causing hypocapnia
questions.e: If ICP is raised and surgery is unavailable, hyperventilation to hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction and gives short-term benefit only.

steps.x: Raised ICP, surgery delayed.

elim: It can be used as a short-term bridge.
It gives only short-term benefit.
Hypercapnia raises ICP by vasodilatation.
It has no effect on clotting.

steps.x: D: It lowers ICP for a short time only by causing hypocapnia. Hyperventilation (low CO2): short-term ICP bridge only.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman taking dabigatran for atrial fibrillation falls and develops an acute subdural haemorrhage. Her GCS is 13. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm and irregular and BP 154/86 mmHg. Her last dose was 4 hours ago. Neurosurgery plans to operate.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line reversal agent?
questions.e: In intracranial haemorrhage on dabigatran, first-line reversal is idarucizumab, a monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran.

steps.x: Subdural on a direct thrombin inhibitor.

elim: Reverses factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban.
Reverses warfarin only.
Dabigatran does not affect platelets.
Reverses heparin.

steps.x: B: Idarucizumab. Dabigatran reversal = idarucizumab.

questions.stem: An 86 year old man taking warfarin is seen at home by his GP. His wife says that over 3 days he has become confused at times and sleepy, and he fell in the garden last week. His GCS is 13. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 148/82 mmHg. His urine dipstick is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Arrange emergency hospital admission for a CT head
Stop warfarin and review in 48 hours
questions.e: An anticoagulated older patient with a fall and fluctuating confusion and drowsiness needs urgent non-contrast CT head to exclude subdural haemorrhage.

clues: fell in the garden last week
steps.x: Anticoagulated, fall, fluctuating GCS, at home.

elim: No evidence of infection, and this ignores the fall on warfarin.
Fluctuating drowsiness is not dementia.
A bleed could expand meanwhile.
He needs urgent imaging, not a delay.

steps.x: A: Arrange emergency hospital admission for a CT head. Falls + anticoagulant + confusion: emergency CT head.

questions.stem: An 80 year old woman taking warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve has a significant acute subdural haemorrhage. She is given IV vitamin K 5 mg and 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate before surgery. Her INR was 4.2. A pharmacist asks the student which clotting factors the concentrate replaces.
questions.q: Which clotting factors does 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate replace?
questions.e: Warfarin blocks the vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX and X; 4-factor PCC replaces them immediately and IV vitamin K 5 mg sustains the reversal.

steps.x: Warfarin depletes vitamin K-dependent factors.

elim: Fibrinogen and factors V and VIII are not in PCC.
Not the vitamin K-dependent factors.
That is recombinant factor VIIa.
Used in haemophilia A and von Willebrand disease.

steps.x: B: II, VII, IX and X. 4-factor PCC = II, VII, IX, X.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man's CT head shows a crescentic collection spreading over the whole of the left hemisphere, crossing the coronal and lambdoid sutures. A student asks why it is not confined between sutures like the extradural haematoma she saw last week. His GCS is 14.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation?
o: The arachnoid is firmly fused to the skull at sutures
The collection is arterial and under high pressure
The collection is in the subarachnoid space
The subdural space has no attachment of the dura to particular bones, so blood spreads freely
The sutures are fused in the elderly
questions.e: Blood in the subdural space is not limited by the dura's attachments to bone at the sutures, so it spreads freely, forms a crescent and crosses sutures; extradural blood strips the dura from the skull and stops at sutures.

clues: crossing the coronal and lambdoid sutures
steps.x: Why does a subdural cross sutures?

elim: The arachnoid is not attached to the skull.
Subdural bleeding is venous and low pressure.
Subarachnoid blood fills sulci and cisterns, not a crescent.
Extradurals are still limited by sutures in adults; the space is the difference.

steps.x: D: The subdural space has no attachment of the dura to particular bones, so blood spreads freely. Subdural: no bony attachment, so crescent and crosses sutures.

questions.stem: An 85 year old woman has a chronic subdural haemorrhage that has been followed with CT. Over 6 weeks it has become darker than brain on CT and has slowly increased in size. Her GCS is 15 and she has a mild headache. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 140/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for these changes?
o: CSF leaking from the subarachnoid space only
Liquefaction of the clot with neomembrane formation and repeated small rebleeds
Ongoing arterial bleeding from the middle meningeal artery
questions.e: A chronic subdural undergoes progressive liquefaction (becoming hypodense) and forms neomembranes whose fragile vessels rebleed, causing gradual enlargement.

steps.x: Chronic subdural becoming hypodense and larger.

elim: Not the mechanism of a chronic subdural.
Would cause fever and a rim-enhancing empyema.
That causes extradural haemorrhage.
Would make it brighter, not darker.

steps.x: C: Liquefaction of the clot with neomembrane formation and repeated small rebleeds. Chronic subdural: liquefaction, neomembranes, rebleeding.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man taking apixaban has an acute subdural haemorrhage after a fall. His GCS is 14. The consultant asks the team to reverse the anticoagulant immediately, before the neurosurgical decision is made. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 150/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the main reason for prioritising reversal?
o: Ongoing anticoagulation increases haematoma expansion and worsens outcome
Reversal treats the underlying atrial fibrillation
questions.e: Ongoing anticoagulant effect significantly increases the risk of haematoma expansion and worse neurological outcome, so reversal comes first.

steps.x: Why reverse first?

elim: They do not.
It has no effect on imaging.
Not the purpose of reversal.
It removes stroke protection; it does not treat AF.

steps.x: C: Ongoing anticoagulation increases haematoma expansion and worsens outcome. Anticoagulation drives haematoma expansion: reverse early.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man and an 80 year old man are both admitted after head injuries. The young man has an extradural haemorrhage and deteriorates within 3 hours. The older man has cerebral atrophy and a subdural haemorrhage, and his symptoms develop gradually over 2 weeks. A student asks why the subdural took so long to cause symptoms.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation?
o: Atrophy prevents any rise in intracranial pressure
CSF in the subdural space dilutes the blood
Subdural blood is limited by suture lines
The bleeding is arterial from the middle meningeal artery
The bleeding is venous, so it accumulates slowly
questions.e: Subdural haemorrhage is venous (bridging veins) and low pressure, so it accumulates more slowly than arterial extradural bleeds; brain atrophy also leaves room before symptoms appear.

steps.x: Compare the timing of extradural and subdural bleeds.

elim: Atrophy leaves space, but pressure still rises as the clot grows.
CSF lies in the subarachnoid space.
Subdurals cross suture lines.
That is the extradural haemorrhage.

steps.x: E: The bleeding is venous, so it accumulates slowly. Venous bleed = slow and fluctuating; arterial (extradural) = rapid.
